transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, thank you. I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that my eating has been all over the place lately. Like, some weeks I barely touch dinner at all. And then other nights I just stand in the kitchen eating crackers and sweets after everyone's gone to bed. It’s so quiet then, you know? The hum of the refrigerator is actually really soothing. I bought this new brand of crackers last week, the ones with the little seeds on top? They were on sale at the grocery store. I always try to go on Tuesdays because that’s when they restock the produce, and the lady at the checkout—she has this really interesting accent, I think she said she’s from Eastern Europe somewhere—she always remembers that I bring my own bags. But yeah, my appetite is just... it's really unpredictable right now.

When you're eating those crackers and sweets late at night, do you feel like you're eating a much larger amount than most people would eat, and do you feel like you can't stop or control how much you're eating during those times?

Um, no, not really. It's not a huge amount, just like... a few handfuls, I guess? I can stop whenever I want. It's just nice to have something to crunch on. I really hate how they package those cracker sleeves, by the way. You try to open just the top and the clear plastic tears all the way down the side, and then they go stale so fast. 

I actually tried putting them in one of those plastic storage containers—the ones with the little snap-on lids? My sister got me a whole matching set of them for my birthday a couple of years ago. She always buys really practical gifts like that. Which is fine, I mean, they are useful, but sometimes you just want something pretty, you know? Like a nice scarf or maybe a good book. I used to read so much when I was taking classes at the community college. I had this one literature professor who made us read all these obscure Russian novels... wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, the eating at night. Yeah, no, I don't feel out of control or anything like that. I just eat a little bit and then go to bed.
Over the past few weeks or months, how would you describe your overall mood? Have you been feeling sad, empty, or down most of the time?

Well, yeah, I do go through these stretches where everything just feels... I don't know, heavy? Like the whole house is just gray. I'll just sit there at the kitchen table feeling completely empty, even when nothing bad has even happened that day. I have this nice little table, actually, it’s oak. I found it at a garage sale a few years ago. The guy selling it was moving to Florida, I think? He said he was retiring to be closer to his grandkids. It’s funny how people just pack up their whole lives and move somewhere so humid. I don't think I could handle the humidity down there. My hair gets so frizzy just when it rains here. I tried this new conditioner that was supposed to help with frizz, but it smelled like artificial coconut. You know that smell? Like sunscreen? It always reminds me of going to the community pool when I was a kid. We used to ride our bikes there every afternoon... but anyway, yeah, I just sit at that oak table and feel really down for no real reason.
When you describe feeling heavy and empty at the kitchen table, how many days per week would you say you feel that way, and has this been going on for at least two weeks?

Um, yeah, I'd say it's been going on for a while now. Definitely more than two weeks. It's like I said, I go through these stretches where the whole house just feels so gray and heavy, and I'll just sit at the kitchen table feeling completely empty, even though nothing terrible has happened that day. It happens almost every day, maybe five or six days a week? 

I usually sit there with a mug of tea. I have this really pretty ceramic mug that I got at a craft fair last summer. The glaze on it is this gorgeous deep blue, almost like the ocean. The woman who made it was telling me all about her kiln and how the temperature affects the colors. She had this huge setup in her backyard. I always thought it would be nice to have a hobby like that, you know? Making things with your hands. I tried knitting once, but I could never get the tension right. My stitches were always way too tight, and then I'd drop one and the whole thing would unravel. It was so frustrating. I ended up giving all my yarn to a neighbor who makes those little hats for premature babies at the hospital. Such a sweet thing to do, right? But anyway, yeah, it's been most days of the week for a few weeks now, just feeling really empty.

Besides feeling empty and heavy, have you noticed that things you used to enjoy doing—like reading those Russian novels you mentioned, or other hobbies or activities—don't bring you pleasure or interest anymore?

Yeah, it's exactly like that. Things I used to really look forward to, like my book club or cooking... or going to art galleries, they just feel like chores now. I just keep putting them off. 

Speaking of galleries, there was this little one downtown that used to have these amazing watercolor exhibits. The artist was local, and she used this really specific type of thick, cold-pressed paper that gave the paintings this incredible texture. Paper making is actually a fascinating process, if you ever look into it. The Egyptians used papyrus, obviously, but modern paper has all that wood pulp. That's why old books get that sweet, almost vanilla smell, you know? It's the lignin breaking down. I absolutely love the smell of old books. My local library had a huge book sale last month where you could fill up a whole paper grocery bag for a dollar. I bought three bags, but they're still just sitting in the trunk of my car. 

My car has been making this awful rattling noise anyway, right near the muffler, and I really need to take it in to the shop. The mechanic I usually go to is always so booked up, though. He has this calendar on his wall with classic cars on it, like old Mustangs and Corvettes... but um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, not enjoying things. Yeah, even tending my rose beds out back. I used to spend hours out there, but lately, just the thought of going out with the pruning shears feels like so much work, so I just avoid it.

Over these past few weeks when you're feeling this heaviness and emptiness, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—like sleeping much more than usual, or having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep?

Um, my sleep? I don't know, I haven't really noticed any big changes. I guess I just sleep like I usually do. I do have this really heavy comforter on my bed, though. It's one of those weighted blankets? My sister got it for me for my birthday last year. She said it was supposed to help with anxiety, but honestly, it just makes me feel pinned down sometimes. 

She's always buying me these trendy health things. Like last month, she sent me a box of that matcha powder. Have you ever tried that? It's supposed to be so good for you, all those antioxidants, but it tastes like grass clippings. I tried making a latte with it using almond milk, but the powder just clumped up at the bottom of the mug. The same blue mug I was telling you about earlier, actually. It's so hard to whisk that stuff properly unless you have one of those little bamboo whisks. I saw a video online of someone using one in this traditional Japanese tea ceremony, and it looked so peaceful. They have these beautiful rock gardens there, where they just rake the sand into these perfect, even lines. I always thought that would be so meditative, just raking sand all day. But anyway, no, my sleep hasn't really been any different lately.
Over these past few weeks when you're feeling this heaviness and emptiness, have you noticed that you feel more tired or fatigued than usual, even when you've had enough sleep?

Um, tired? No, I don't think I've felt any more tired than usual. I mean, the heaviness is there, but it's not like a physical exhaustion, you know? 

Speaking of feeling tired, though, my neighbor's dog has been barking so much lately, right by the fence. It's this little terrier mix, and it just yaps at everything that goes by. The mail carrier, squirrels, the wind... I don't know how they stand it. They have this huge oak tree in their front yard, and the acorns are starting to fall. They make such a loud popping sound when they hit the roof of my car. I really need to get that rattling noise checked out, like I said. But the acorns, they just cover the driveway. I tried sweeping them up the other day, but the broom I have is one of those cheap plastic ones, and the bristles are all bent. I really should get a nice straw broom. My grandmother used to have one, and she'd sweep her front porch every single morning. She lived in this beautiful old Victorian house with a wraparound porch. It had a porch swing that creaked every time you moved. But no, I haven't really noticed feeling more fatigued or anything like that.
Besides the heaviness and emptiness you've described, have you been experiencing a lot of worry or anxiety about things? Do you find yourself feeling tense, nervous, or on edge most days?

Worry or anxiety? No, I don't think so. I haven't really been feeling tense or on edge at all. 

My sister is the one who's always on edge, honestly. She's constantly worrying about her cats. She has these three rescue cats, and she's always terrified they're going to get out of the house. One of them, Barnaby, he's this big orange tabby, and he is an absolute escape artist. He actually figured out how to push the screen door open on her back patio. Screens are so flimsy these days anyway, aren't they? I remember when I was a kid, we had this heavy metal screen door on our kitchen, and it had this strong spring on it. It would slam shut with this loud *thwack* sound every single time. You could hear it from all the way down the street. 

We used to run in and out of that door all summer long, catching fireflies in old glass mayonnaise jars. My mom would poke holes in the metal lids with an ice pick so the bugs could breathe. Ice picks are kind of scary-looking tools when you think about it. You never really see them in kitchens anymore, probably because refrigerators all have those built-in ice makers now. Mine has been acting up, actually, the ice comes out all crushed even when I press the button for cubed. But um, yeah, to answer your question, I haven't been feeling nervous or worried myself.
When you're sitting at the kitchen table feeling that heaviness and emptiness, do you notice that you're moving more slowly than usual, or does it feel like your body is sluggish and hard to move?

Moving slower? No, I don't think I'm moving any slower than I usually do. The heaviness is just... there, but my body moves fine. 

Although, speaking of sitting at the kitchen table, the chairs I have are those wooden spindle ones? They look nice, but they are incredibly uncomfortable if you sit in them too long. I bought these little tie-on cushions for them from a catalog last spring. The catalog had all these gardening supplies in it, too. I kept looking at the raised planter boxes they were selling. I've always wanted to grow my own tomatoes, the big heirloom ones that get all bumpy and weird-looking. They taste so much better than the perfectly round ones at the grocery store. The grocery store near me actually rearranged their entire produce section last week, and it took me twenty minutes just to find the carrots. They moved all the root vegetables to this weird corner display that looks like a little farmer's cart. It even has these fake wooden wagon wheels on the sides. Wagon wheels are so heavy, I can't imagine how people used to fix them when they broke on the Oregon Trail or whatever. But no, I haven't noticed feeling sluggish or moving slowly at all.
During these times when you're feeling empty and heavy, do you find yourself having negative thoughts about yourself—like feeling worthless, guilty about things, or blaming yourself for problems?

Guilty? Yeah, I do get like that. When that heavy feeling hits, I can spend hours just sitting there replaying these tiny little things. Like, last week I bought this expensive tube of cobalt blue pigment for my painting, or maybe I snapped at my husband over something silly, and suddenly I feel like I've completely ruined the whole household because of it. It just spirals. 

Speaking of painting, I haven't even opened that cobalt blue yet. The tube is still sitting on my easel. My easel is right by the window in the spare room, and the afternoon light comes in so perfectly there. But the window has this draft, you know? I really need to get some weather stripping for it. The hardware store down the street sells it by the roll, but their parking lot is a nightmare. It's so tiny, and people just leave their carts wherever they want. I saw a cart roll right into the side of a red pickup truck the other day. It left a huge scratch. I'd be so mad if someone scratched my car like that, especially since I still need to get that rattling noise checked out. My mechanic is always so busy, though. He has this calendar on his wall with classic cars on it, and the one for this month is a 1957 Chevy Bel Air. They don't make cars with fins like that anymore, do they? But um, yeah, I definitely get stuck feeling really guilty and worthless over the smallest things.
Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating, making decisions, or keeping your thoughts organized over these past few weeks?

Concentrating? No, I don't think I've had any trouble with that. I can focus just fine when I need to. 

Like when I was reading this book the other day, I sat there for hours just completely absorbed in it. It was this mystery novel set in a small coastal town in Maine. I've always wanted to visit Maine, especially in the fall when the leaves change colors. I bet the reds and oranges are just spectacular up there. We don't really get that kind of autumn foliage around here, just a lot of brown leaves that end up clogging the gutters. My husband is supposed to clean the gutters out this weekend, actually. He bought this special attachment for the hose that's supposed to blast the leaves out, but I'm pretty sure it's just going to make a huge muddy mess all over the side of the house. The siding is a really light beige, so dirt shows up on it so easily. We had it pressure washed a few years ago by this guy who drove a van with a giant cartoon bubble painted on the side. The bubble had a little smiley face in it. It's funny the things people put on their work vehicles, isn't it? But yeah, no, my concentration and making decisions and all that has been perfectly fine.
Have people close to you, like your husband, mentioned that you've been talking more slowly than usual, or that you seem to be doing things at a slower pace than you normally do?

Talking slower? No, my husband hasn't said anything like that to me. I think I'm talking at my normal speed, and I haven't noticed anyone looking at me funny like I'm dragging my words out or anything. 

He did mention the other day that I talk a lot when I'm excited, though. We were at the garden center looking for those heirloom tomato seeds I mentioned before. The garden center is massive, it has these huge greenhouse sections that smell like wet dirt and fertilizer. It's a very specific smell, you know? It always reminds me of my grandfather's potting shed. He used to keep all his tools hanging on this pegboard that he painted bright yellow. I don't know why yellow, maybe so he could see the outlines of the tools better? He drew little black outlines around every single wrench and trowel so he knew exactly where they went back. I wish I was that organized. My kitchen drawers are just a jumble of spatulas and measuring spoons. I can never find the one-third cup measure when I need it. I was trying to bake oatmeal cookies last week, the kind with the raisins in them, and I had to guess the measurements. They turned out a little flat, to be honest. But they still tasted good with a glass of cold milk. But um, no, nobody has said I'm moving or talking slower than usual.
When you're sitting at that kitchen table feeling heavy and empty, do people ever have to ask you to repeat yourself, or do they seem to be waiting for you to finish your sentences?

Repeat myself? No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anyone waiting for me to finish a sentence or anything like that. 

Usually when I'm sitting at the table like that, it's pretty quiet anyway. The kitchen gets this really nice morning light, especially near the sink. I have this little row of succulents lined up on the windowsill there. They're supposed to be really hard to kill, but one of them is starting to look a little brown around the edges. I think maybe I overwatered it. It's in this tiny little terracotta pot that I painted with white polka dots. I used a Q-tip to make the dots, actually. It's a neat little trick I saw on one of those craft shows on TV. The host was making these elaborate centerpieces for a wedding, using all these silk flowers. I don't really like silk flowers, though. They always get so dusty, and trying to clean them is a nightmare. You have to take a hair dryer to them on the cool setting, otherwise you just smear the dust around. My hair dryer has been acting up lately, actually. It makes this high-pitched whining noise right before it gets really hot. I should probably just throw it out and buy a new one before it catches fire or something. But yeah, no, I don't think anyone has to wait for me to finish talking or ask me to repeat things.

Has your husband or anyone else close to you mentioned that you seem to be speaking more slowly than you used to, or that there's more of a pause between when you start talking and when the words come out?

No, he hasn't said anything like that. I really don't think I'm talking any slower than I usually do. Honestly, if anything, I think I talk too fast sometimes, especially when I get on the phone with my sister. 

She lives out in Seattle, so we only talk maybe once a week because of the time difference. It's always raining when I talk to her. I don't know how she handles all that rain, I think I'd go crazy. She bought this really nice raincoat, though, bright yellow, kind of like my grandfather's pegboard I was talking about earlier. It has these deep pockets that she says are perfect for carrying her dog's treats. She has a golden retriever named Buster. He's such a sweet dog, but he sheds everywhere. I couldn't deal with the dog hair. I have a hard enough time keeping the floors clean with just me and my husband. We have hardwood floors in the living room, and every speck of dust shows up on them. I was trying to find a good mop the other day, one of those ones with the washable pads? But there were so many options at the store, I just got overwhelmed and left without buying one. I ended up just using a damp towel and pushing it around with my foot. It worked okay, I guess. But um... no, I haven't noticed any pauses or talking slower, and my husband hasn't mentioned it either.

patient.answer:
Um, yeah, I'd say it's been going on for a while now. Definitely more than two weeks. It's like I said, I go through these stretches where the whole house just feels so gray and heavy, and I'll just sit at the kitchen table feeling completely empty, even though nothing terrible has happened that day. It happens almost every day, maybe five or six days a week? 

I usually sit there with a mug of tea. I have this really pretty ceramic mug that I got at a craft fair last summer. The glaze on it is this gorgeous deep blue, almost like the ocean. The woman who made it was telling me all about her kiln and how the temperature affects the colors. She had this huge setup in her backyard. I always thought it would be nice to have a hobby like that, you know? Making things with your hands. I tried knitting once, but I could never get the tension right. My stitches were always way too tight, and then I'd drop one and the whole thing would unravel. It was so frustrating. I ended up giving all my yarn to a neighbor who makes those little hats for premature babies at the hospital. Such a sweet thing to do, right? But anyway, yeah, it's been most days of the week for a few weeks now, just feeling really empty.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure in activities) to help differentiate Major Depressive Disorder from Generalized Anxiety Disorder
doctor.question: Besides feeling empty and heavy, have you noticed that things you used to enjoy doing—like reading those Russian novels you mentioned, or other hobbies or activities—don't bring you pleasure or interest anymore?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: Things I used to look forward to, like book club, cooking, galleries, and tending the rose beds, can just feel like chores I keep putting off.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I have lost interest or pleasure in activities I used to enjoy, which corresponds to the Loss of Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it's exactly like that. Things I used to really look forward to, like my book club or cooking... or going to art galleries, they just feel like chores now. I just keep putting them off. 

Speaking of galleries, there was this little one downtown that used to have these amazing watercolor exhibits. The artist was local, and she used this really specific type of thick, cold-pressed paper that gave the paintings this incredible texture. Paper making is actually a fascinating process, if you ever look into it. The Egyptians used papyrus, obviously, but modern paper has all that wood pulp. That's why old books get that sweet, almost vanilla smell, you know? It's the lignin breaking down. I absolutely love the smell of old books. My local library had a huge book sale last month where you could fill up a whole paper grocery bag for a dollar. I bought three bags, but they're still just sitting in the trunk of my car. 

My car has been making this awful rattling noise anyway, right near the muffler, and I really need to take it in to the shop. The mechanic I usually go to is always so booked up, though. He has this calendar on his wall with classic cars on it, like old Mustangs and Corvettes... but um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, not enjoying things. Yeah, even tending my rose beds out back. I used to spend hours out there, but lately, just the thought of going out with the pruning shears feels like so much work, so I just avoid it.

inference.note: Anhedonia (loss of pleasure in previously enjoyed activities like book club, cooking, galleries, gardening) combined with persistent depressed mood (5-6 days/week for several weeks), psychomotor symptoms (avoidance, putting things off), and vegetative symptoms (variable appetite) strongly support Major Depressive Disorder. The patient's tangential speech and flight of ideas are consistent with depression, not anxiety. F41.9 (Anxiety Disorder) ruled out as primary diagnosis given clear anhedonia and depressive symptoms predominating over anxiety symptoms.

doctor.intent: Assess for anhedonia persistence and severity to confirm major depressive disorder diagnosis, and to differentiate from other conditions. Also need to rule out the possibility that the patient's tangential speech pattern and difficulty maintaining focus might indicate a different condition.
doctor.question: Over these past few weeks when you're feeling this heaviness and emptiness, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—like sleeping much more than usual, or having trouble falling asleep or staying asleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about insomnia or hypersomnia during depressive episodes, which is not covered in my symptom profile. The only sleep-related item I have is decreased need for sleep during manic episodes.

patient.answer:
Um, my sleep? I don't know, I haven't really noticed any big changes. I guess I just sleep like I usually do. I do have this really heavy comforter on my bed, though. It's one of those weighted blankets? My sister got it for me for my birthday last year. She said it was supposed to help with anxiety, but honestly, it just makes me feel pinned down sometimes. 

She's always buying me these trendy health things. Like last month, she sent me a box of that matcha powder. Have you ever tried that? It's supposed to be so good for you, all those antioxidants, but it tastes like grass clippings. I tried making a latte with it using almond milk, but the powder just clumped up at the bottom of the mug. The same blue mug I was telling you about earlier, actually. It's so hard to whisk that stuff properly unless you have one of those little bamboo whisks. I saw a video online of someone using one in this traditional Japanese tea ceremony, and it looked so peaceful. They have these beautiful rock gardens there, where they just rake the sand into these perfect, even lines. I always thought that would be so meditative, just raking sand all day. But anyway, no, my sleep hasn't really been any different lately.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced significant changes in energy level, fatigue, or ability to concentrate, which would help confirm a major depressive episode and rule out other conditions
doctor.question: Over these past few weeks when you're feeling this heaviness and emptiness, have you noticed that you feel more tired or fatigued than usual, even when you've had enough sleep?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fatigue or loss of energy, which is not present in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Um, tired? No, I don't think I've felt any more tired than usual. I mean, the heaviness is there, but it's not like a physical exhaustion, you know? 

Speaking of feeling tired, though, my neighbor's dog has been barking so much lately, right by the fence. It's this little terrier mix, and it just yaps at everything that goes by. The mail carrier, squirrels, the wind... I don't know how they stand it. They have this huge oak tree in their front yard, and the acorns are starting to fall. They make such a loud popping sound when they hit the roof of my car. I really need to get that rattling noise checked out, like I said. But the acorns, they just cover the driveway. I tried sweeping them up the other day, but the broom I have is one of those cheap plastic ones, and the bristles are all bent. I really should get a nice straw broom. My grandmother used to have one, and she'd sweep her front porch every single morning. She lived in this beautiful old Victorian house with a wraparound porch. It had a porch swing that creaked every time you moved. But no, I haven't really noticed feeling more fatigued or anything like that.

inference.note: Added F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) as a candidate. Patient demonstrates significant tangential thinking and flight of ideas throughout responses, plus persistent worry-like rumination patterns. However, core depressive symptoms (anhedonia, depressed mood 5-6 days/week for >2 weeks, emptiness) remain primary. Sleep and fatigue denial is notable but not definitive. The marked circumstantial speech with difficulty maintaining focus on questions suggests possible anxiety component or attention issues alongside depression.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences anxiety symptoms (worry, tension, physical symptoms of anxiety) that would support F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder) versus depression alone (F32.9)
doctor.question: Besides the heaviness and emptiness you've described, have you been experiencing a lot of worry or anxiety about things? Do you find yourself feeling tense, nervous, or on edge most days?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of anxiety, worry, or feeling tense/on edge, which are not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Worry or anxiety? No, I don't think so. I haven't really been feeling tense or on edge at all. 

My sister is the one who's always on edge, honestly. She's constantly worrying about her cats. She has these three rescue cats, and she's always terrified they're going to get out of the house. One of them, Barnaby, he's this big orange tabby, and he is an absolute escape artist. He actually figured out how to push the screen door open on her back patio. Screens are so flimsy these days anyway, aren't they? I remember when I was a kid, we had this heavy metal screen door on our kitchen, and it had this strong spring on it. It would slam shut with this loud *thwack* sound every single time. You could hear it from all the way down the street. 

We used to run in and out of that door all summer long, catching fireflies in old glass mayonnaise jars. My mom would poke holes in the metal lids with an ice pick so the bugs could breathe. Ice picks are kind of scary-looking tools when you think about it. You never really see them in kitchens anymore, probably because refrigerators all have those built-in ice makers now. Mine has been acting up, actually, the ice comes out all crushed even when I press the button for cubed. But um, yeah, to answer your question, I haven't been feeling nervous or worried myself.

inference.note: Ruled out F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder). Patient explicitly denies anxiety, worry, tension, and feeling on edge. Meets criteria for Major Depressive Disorder: depressed mood 5-6 days/week for several weeks, anhedonia (loss of interest in reading, book club, cooking, galleries, gardening), but denies fatigue and sleep changes. The tangential speech with excessive detail is notable but patient denies anxiety symptoms required for GAD diagnosis.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has psychomotor changes (agitation or retardation) associated with depression, which would help confirm Major Depressive Disorder and rule out other conditions
doctor.question: When you're sitting at the kitchen table feeling that heaviness and emptiness, do you notice that you're moving more slowly than usual, or does it feel like your body is sluggish and hard to move?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving slowly or feeling sluggish), which is not covered by any of the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Moving slower? No, I don't think I'm moving any slower than I usually do. The heaviness is just... there, but my body moves fine. 

Although, speaking of sitting at the kitchen table, the chairs I have are those wooden spindle ones? They look nice, but they are incredibly uncomfortable if you sit in them too long. I bought these little tie-on cushions for them from a catalog last spring. The catalog had all these gardening supplies in it, too. I kept looking at the raised planter boxes they were selling. I've always wanted to grow my own tomatoes, the big heirloom ones that get all bumpy and weird-looking. They taste so much better than the perfectly round ones at the grocery store. The grocery store near me actually rearranged their entire produce section last week, and it took me twenty minutes just to find the carrots. They moved all the root vegetables to this weird corner display that looks like a little farmer's cart. It even has these fake wooden wagon wheels on the sides. Wagon wheels are so heavy, I can't imagine how people used to fix them when they broke on the Oregon Trail or whatever. But no, I haven't noticed feeling sluggish or moving slowly at all.

doctor.intent: Assess for feelings of worthlessness, guilt, or self-blame, which are core symptoms of Major Depressive Disorder that haven't been directly explored yet
doctor.question: During these times when you're feeling empty and heavy, do you find yourself having negative thoughts about yourself—like feeling worthless, guilty about things, or blaming yourself for problems?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I can spend hours replaying small things, like buying an expensive tube of pigment or snapping at my spouse, and feel like I’ve ruined the whole household because of it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness, guilt, or self-blame, which directly corresponds to the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Guilty? Yeah, I do get like that. When that heavy feeling hits, I can spend hours just sitting there replaying these tiny little things. Like, last week I bought this expensive tube of cobalt blue pigment for my painting, or maybe I snapped at my husband over something silly, and suddenly I feel like I've completely ruined the whole household because of it. It just spirals. 

Speaking of painting, I haven't even opened that cobalt blue yet. The tube is still sitting on my easel. My easel is right by the window in the spare room, and the afternoon light comes in so perfectly there. But the window has this draft, you know? I really need to get some weather stripping for it. The hardware store down the street sells it by the roll, but their parking lot is a nightmare. It's so tiny, and people just leave their carts wherever they want. I saw a cart roll right into the side of a red pickup truck the other day. It left a huge scratch. I'd be so mad if someone scratched my car like that, especially since I still need to get that rattling noise checked out. My mechanic is always so busy, though. He has this calendar on his wall with classic cars on it, and the one for this month is a 1957 Chevy Bel Air. They don't make cars with fins like that anymore, do they? But um, yeah, I definitely get stuck feeling really guilty and worthless over the smallest things.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient has experienced significant changes in concentration or ability to make decisions, which would help differentiate between Major Depressive Disorder and other conditions, and also help assess severity.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any difficulty concentrating, making decisions, or keeping your thoughts organized over these past few weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness (a depressive symptom). This specific symptom is not in my profile.

patient.answer:
Concentrating? No, I don't think I've had any trouble with that. I can focus just fine when I need to. 

Like when I was reading this book the other day, I sat there for hours just completely absorbed in it. It was this mystery novel set in a small coastal town in Maine. I've always wanted to visit Maine, especially in the fall when the leaves change colors. I bet the reds and oranges are just spectacular up there. We don't really get that kind of autumn foliage around here, just a lot of brown leaves that end up clogging the gutters. My husband is supposed to clean the gutters out this weekend, actually. He bought this special attachment for the hose that's supposed to blast the leaves out, but I'm pretty sure it's just going to make a huge muddy mess all over the side of the house. The siding is a really light beige, so dirt shows up on it so easily. We had it pressure washed a few years ago by this guy who drove a van with a giant cartoon bubble painted on the side. The bubble had a little smiley face in it. It's funny the things people put on their work vehicles, isn't it? But yeah, no, my concentration and making decisions and all that has been perfectly fine.

doctor.intent: Assess for psychomotor retardation or agitation as a depressive symptom, since the patient denied fatigue and slowness but I need to clarify if there are observable changes in speech rate, activity level, or mental processing speed that they may not have consciously noticed.
doctor.question: Have people close to you, like your husband, mentioned that you've been talking more slowly than usual, or that you seem to be doing things at a slower pace than you normally do?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about observable psychomotor retardation (talking or moving more slowly as noticed by others), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Talking slower? No, my husband hasn't said anything like that to me. I think I'm talking at my normal speed, and I haven't noticed anyone looking at me funny like I'm dragging my words out or anything. 

He did mention the other day that I talk a lot when I'm excited, though. We were at the garden center looking for those heirloom tomato seeds I mentioned before. The garden center is massive, it has these huge greenhouse sections that smell like wet dirt and fertilizer. It's a very specific smell, you know? It always reminds me of my grandfather's potting shed. He used to keep all his tools hanging on this pegboard that he painted bright yellow. I don't know why yellow, maybe so he could see the outlines of the tools better? He drew little black outlines around every single wrench and trowel so he knew exactly where they went back. I wish I was that organized. My kitchen drawers are just a jumble of spatulas and measuring spoons. I can never find the one-third cup measure when I need it. I was trying to bake oatmeal cookies last week, the kind with the raisins in them, and I had to guess the measurements. They turned out a little flat, to be honest. But they still tasted good with a glass of cold milk. But um, no, nobody has said I'm moving or talking slower than usual.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has psychomotor retardation (slowed speech/movement) by asking a more direct, observable question, since they denied it when asked about themselves but may not have accurate self-awareness. This helps differentiate F32.9 (MDD) with psychomotor features from other presentations.
doctor.question: When you're sitting at that kitchen table feeling heavy and empty, do people ever have to ask you to repeat yourself, or do they seem to be waiting for you to finish your sentences?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about poverty of speech, thought blocking, or psychomotor retardation (people waiting for the patient to finish sentences or repeating themselves), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Repeat myself? No, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anyone waiting for me to finish a sentence or anything like that. 

Usually when I'm sitting at the table like that, it's pretty quiet anyway. The kitchen gets this really nice morning light, especially near the sink. I have this little row of succulents lined up on the windowsill there. They're supposed to be really hard to kill, but one of them is starting to look a little brown around the edges. I think maybe I overwatered it. It's in this tiny little terracotta pot that I painted with white polka dots. I used a Q-tip to make the dots, actually. It's a neat little trick I saw on one of those craft shows on TV. The host was making these elaborate centerpieces for a wedding, using all these silk flowers. I don't really like silk flowers, though. They always get so dusty, and trying to clean them is a nightmare. You have to take a hair dryer to them on the cool setting, otherwise you just smear the dust around. My hair dryer has been acting up lately, actually. It makes this high-pitched whining noise right before it gets really hot. I should probably just throw it out and buy a new one before it catches fire or something. But yeah, no, I don't think anyone has to wait for me to finish talking or ask me to repeat things.

doctor.intent: Assess for psychomotor retardation by asking about objective observable signs that others would notice, specifically whether the patient's speech pace has slowed down as reported by others
doctor.question: Has your husband or anyone else close to you mentioned that you seem to be speaking more slowly than you used to, or that there's more of a pause between when you start talking and when the words come out?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (speaking more slowly or with delays), which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, he hasn't said anything like that. I really don't think I'm talking any slower than I usually do. Honestly, if anything, I think I talk too fast sometimes, especially when I get on the phone with my sister. 

She lives out in Seattle, so we only talk maybe once a week because of the time difference. It's always raining when I talk to her. I don't know how she handles all that rain, I think I'd go crazy. She bought this really nice raincoat, though, bright yellow, kind of like my grandfather's pegboard I was talking about earlier. It has these deep pockets that she says are perfect for carrying her dog's treats. She has a golden retriever named Buster. He's such a sweet dog, but he sheds everywhere. I couldn't deal with the dog hair. I have a hard enough time keeping the floors clean with just me and my husband. We have hardwood floors in the living room, and every speck of dust shows up on them. I was trying to find a good mop the other day, one of those ones with the washable pads? But there were so many options at the store, I just got overwhelmed and left without buying one. I ended up just using a damp towel and pushing it around with my foot. It worked okay, I guess. But um... no, I haven't noticed any pauses or talking slower, and my husband hasn't mentioned it either.
